rdra.haloHtml:
Near 0.93 µm, the light in a ring 31″ to 49″ from R Draconis’s centre, outside the part the frames leave blank, could be measured in 3 of 3 looks, taken on 3 visits. A curve is drawn only from looks on at least 3 visits, all within 0.005 µm of colour; these looks do not meet that, so each reading is listed instead.

Light in the ring, each look
LookColourRing light vs the median of these looks
0.941 µm−43% ± 3.0%
0.940 µm+11% ± 8.6%
0.917 µm+0.0% ± 8.9%

Measured against 2 nearby comparison stars from Gaia. The ± is each reading’s noise: the sky around the ring and around the comparison stars, and how far off the star’s catalogue position could be. These looks were taken from 0.917 to 0.941 µm; looks at slightly different colours can read differently for that reason alone. 3 catalogued Gaia stars (brightest G 16.2) sit in or at the edge of the ring, so some of their light is in every reading.

  • 18 Jul 2025, 16 Sep 2026: Ring brightness is sensitive to the catalogue position; the error bar includes the stated position uncertainty.

text.title: How faint would Planet Nine be, and how deep do the searches go?
text.caption: The rows are in different bands, so their numbers are not interchangeable. The Planet Nine rows are optical brightness: the chart does not estimate how bright it would be at SPHEREx's wavelengths. This is an estimate from published numbers, not a search result.
notes: Rows are in different bands (optical R and V, survey g, r, i, z and y, SPHEREx AB per channel, WISE W2) on one axis with no colour correction, so compare them only roughly. Only the model row is this repo's own estimate (reflected sunlight, V band); the others come from the papers listed, with the one-observation SPHEREx depth and the WISE 0855 AB value worked out here from published numbers, and the Planet Nine ranges read by eye from Figure 9 of Brown & Batygin 2021.
An estimate only: the one-observation depth assumes four equal independent observations. The model assumes the object is seen at opposition, fully lit.
W2 is a broadband average and WISE 0855's spectrum changes steeply across 3.8 to 5 µm, so its brightness in one SPHEREx channel can differ from W2.
Stacking frames goes deeper for a source that stays put; the gain is not measured here, and shift-and-stack for a moving source is not tested.
Model, V band, if it were at 380 AU (its fitted semi-major axis, not its likely current distance), with albedo 0.475, the middle of the published range.
Together, the ZTF, DES and Pan-STARRS1 searches have ruled out about 78% of the synthetic reference population.

caption: 12 SPHEREx frames from 14 December 2025, taken over about 3.3 hours at wavelengths from 3.96 to 4.36 µm. Each frame sees a different wavelength, so the row mixes colour and time.

The 4 frames from 4.25 to 4.36 µm started within 7 minutes of each other. Among them the core reads 39.2 MJy/sr at 4.25 µm and 1.03 at 4.36 µm. They are close in time, but this card still cannot fully separate colour from time, and the box may sit a little differently on the comet in each frame.

All the pictures share one linear brightness scale, so they can be compared; its top is the brightest pixel in any of the 3×3 boxes. The faint frames look almost black. Anything brighter than the top shows white, such as a star, a hot pixel or a cosmic-ray hit. Pixels with no value in the archive are drawn dark red. The pictures keep the detector’s orientation; they are not turned north up.

The numbers are the mean of the 3×3 pixels at the comet’s predicted position (from IRSA’s Moving Object Search Tool), minus the median of each picture’s border. The box sits on the predicted position, not on the brightest pixel, so it can miss part of the peak. The border is not empty sky: the coma the SPHEREx team reports (about 3 arcminutes in radius) is wider than these pictures (about 4 arcminutes across). They are raw pixel values, not a calibrated measurement.

Here the core is brightest at 4.25 µm (39.2 MJy/sr above its border). The SPHEREx team reports carbon dioxide gas glowing at 4.25 to 4.27 µm in this comet (Lisse et al. 2026). This card does not separate gas light from dust light.
The SPHEREx team reported this comet’s wide carbon dioxide coma (Lisse et al. 2025 and 2026). This card redraws public frames with rough numbers of its own and adds nothing new to that work.
